answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the philosophical position the whole essay is built around attacking. As the passage states directly, it's the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth calls it an assumption precisely because it is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all — it's the unspoken premise behind every claim that a sufficiently advanced chatbot or simulated brain might "wake up."

Although the article doesn't spell out the term's history, computational functionalism descends from the broader philosophical view called functionalism, associated with philosophers like Hilary Putnam in the 1960s: the idea that mental states are defined by their functional or causal role (what they do, how they connect inputs to outputs) rather than by what they're physically made of. Computational functionalism narrows this further by specifying that the relevant functional organization is computational, typically in the Turing-machine sense — meaning a mind running on silicon could in principle be conscious in exactly the way a mind running on neurons is, as long as it implements the same computations.

The article is careful to distinguish this from functionalism more broadly, since later on it notes that these other games in town are all still compatible with what in philosophy is known as functionalism: the idea that properties of mind (including consciousness) depend on the functional organization of the (embodied) brain, while computational functionalism is the much narrower, stronger claim that it's specifically Turing-style algorithmic computation that matters. This is the target Seth spends the next several sections dismantling — his four arguments (brains aren't computers, other non-computational dynamics may matter, life may matter, simulation isn't instantiation) are all aimed at showing why this specific assumption is on shaky ground, even though he's careful to say the fact of the matter remains genuinely uncertain.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the load-bearing assumption that the rest of the essay is going to spend its energy attacking. Seth has just said that the very idea of conscious AI depends on the claim that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Philosophers call that position computational functionalism — and the point of this particular sentence is that it operates less like an argued conclusion and more like a background premise nobody notices they're holding, the water the whole debate swims in.

That's why he flags it as "deeply ingrained" rather than just "widely held." An assumption you can see is one you can argue for or against; an assumption that feels like common sense — because it's baked into how we talk about brains as computers, minds as software — is one that shapes conclusions before any argument even starts. Seth is doing some throat-clearing here before the real work: he immediately adds that if this hidden premise is false, "real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with," and the four numbered arguments that follow (brains aren't computers, other non-Turing forms of computation exist, life may matter, simulation isn't instantiation) are all aimed at prying this assumption loose from its invisibility so it can actually be examined and, in his view, rejected.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, computational functionalism is the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth stresses that this assumption is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all, and that if it's wrong, as he thinks it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr].

It matters because the whole essay is built around testing this one premise. Seth says explicitly that he will summarize four related arguments that undermine the idea that computation, at least of the sort implemented in standard digital computers, is sufficient for consciousness [spya-cv97j7] — these are the "brains are not computers," "other games in town," "life matters," and "simulation is not instantiation" sections that make up the bulk of the piece. Each argument is really an attack on a different piece of computational functionalism: that brains are relevantly like Turing machines, that Turing-style algorithmic computation is the only kind of process that could matter, that non-living substrates could suffice, and that simulating a process is the same as instantiating it.

The term also lets Seth diagnose other people's arguments as smuggling the assumption in rather than defending it. He argues that computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view, and that other theories of consciousness generally sidestep defending computational functionalism, being content instead to assume it [spya-ymbpwn spya-qu7j89]. Even Nick Bostrom's simulation hypothesis, Seth points out, quietly relies on it: it is telling that he notes one necessary assumption, and then just takes it as a given… the assumption that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe]. So the concept functions as the article's central fault line — Seth's case against "conscious AI" is really a case against treating computational functionalism as true by default, rather than a claim that machine consciousness is strictly impossible [spya-rn8y3y].

Autopoiesis is a term coined by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the 1970s to describe the self-maintaining organization characteristic of living systems: a living thing is a network of processes that continuously produces and regenerates its own components, thereby producing and regenerating the very network that produced them, and in doing so constitutes itself as a distinct entity in the space it exists in. The article gives you the etymology directly: "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems."

In context, Seth introduces it right after describing how even a single neuron is "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." The concept does real work later in the essay too: it becomes part of his argument (in the "Life Matters" section) that consciousness may be tied to this self-producing, metabolically active nature of living material rather than to computation as such — he later writes of "the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material" as connecting to the brain's predictive processing.

The point of introducing it here is to sharpen the contrast between brains and computers that this section is building: a silicon chip just sits there running whatever program it's given, but a neuron is constantly rebuilding and sustaining itself as a condition of existing at all. That self-sustaining, self-producing quality — rather than any information-processing capacity — is what autopoiesis names, and it's part of why Seth thinks the "brain as computer" metaphor understates what brains actually are.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a concept from theoretical biology, coined in the 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela (though the article doesn't name them). It describes a system that continuously produces and regenerates its own components and its own organization — a living cell is the paradigm case: it constantly builds and rebuilds its own membrane, proteins and internal structure using energy and matter from outside, in order to keep existing as the same kind of system. The word itself, as the article notes, comes from Greek roots meaning "self-production."

In the passage you've selected, Seth is using the idea to make a specific point in his broader argument against "computational functionalism" (the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness). Just before this parenthetical, he's describing how a single neuron is "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." Autopoiesis names that self-maintaining activity. He then flags it as "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" — meaning this isn't just biological housekeeping, it's plausibly what separates the living from the non-living, including from computers.

This matters for the essay's larger case because a digital computer, however complex its software, does nothing analogous: it doesn't have to continuously regenerate its own hardware to keep computing. So if autopoiesis really is essential to what brains are, that's part of why Seth thinks brains can't be cleanly separated into "software" and "hardware" the way Turing-style computation assumes — which is the whole thrust of the section this passage sits in ("Brains Are Not Computers"). The concept resurfaces later in the essay too, when he links autopoiesis to his "biological naturalism" argument that life itself, not just information processing, may be necessary for consciousness.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, autopoiesis is introduced while Seth is describing just how complicated a single neuron is: "Even a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence. (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)" [spya-cf8rt8]. So here it means the self-producing, self-maintaining activity that keeps a living system in existence — not something a component merely does, but something bound up with what it is.

That distinction is doing real work in the argument against computational functionalism. Seth uses it to explain why brains resist the clean software/hardware split that lets Turing computation be substrate-independent: "This matters because the idea of the brain as a meat-based (universal) Turing machine rests precisely on this sharp separation of scales, on the substrate independence that motivated Turing's definition in the first place. If you cannot separate what brains do from what they are, the mathematical marriage of convenience starts to fall apart, and there is less reason to think of biological wetware as there simply to implement algorithmic mindware." [spya-p4vmm0]. He then applies this directly to the "neural replacement" thought experiment often used to defend substrate independence, arguing that a silicon neuron could never fully substitute for a biological one precisely because of processes like this — his example being neurons that found that some neurons fire spikes of activity apparently to clear waste products created by metabolism, which is exactly the kind of self-maintaining, autopoietic activity a silicon equivalent couldn't replicate [spya-un9fjn].

Autopoiesis resurfaces again in his positive proposal (the "life matters" argument), where he links the cell's self-producing metabolic activity to the predictive, self-regulating processes he thinks underlie conscious experience: "Within these whirls of metabolic activity, the ubiquitous process of prediction error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself. A mathematical line can be drawn directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self." [spya-vys3vj]. So the concept does double duty: it's the biological fact that undermines the brain-as-computer metaphor, and it's the thread Seth tries to use to connect life itself to consciousness.
